homepage.title: Can You Pass This Barrister Entrance Exam?
homepage.summary: Can you track the evidence, test the argument, and stay precise under pressure?
homepage.thumbnailAlt: Scales of justice over a case file for a fictional barrister reasoning challenge

landing.quickStartText: The first cases look simple. Then one word can change the whole argument.

footer.aboutText: This fictional, worldwide-friendly reasoning challenge uses invented cases and self-contained rules to explore evidence reading, precise language, chronology, argument structure, professional judgment, and calm advocacy. It does not teach the law of any country and is not legal advice, legal education, professional training, certification, recruitment screening, or an official barrister assessment.

stageGroups.title: Case File Scan
stageGroups.encouragement: File opened. Now listen for the difference between what was seen and what was assumed.

questions.prompt: The file records: interview 09:10, signed statement 10:05, photograph 10:20. Which happened first?
questions.explanation: 09:10 is earlier than both 10:05 and 10:20.

questions.prompt: A note says, ‘Red folder received at 14:30.’ Which detail is directly recorded?
choices: A red folder was received at 14:30
questions.explanation: Only the folder color, event, and time appear in the note.

questions.prompt: Case summary: Maya entered through Door C; Ivo used Door A. Who used Door C?
questions.explanation: The summary directly links Maya with Door C.

questions.prompt: The file lists four exhibits: map, receipt, key, audio clip. Which item is not listed?
questions.explanation: The listed exhibits do not include a photograph.

questions.prompt: A report changes ‘17 boxes’ to ‘12 boxes’ in a signed correction. Which number should the updated summary use?
questions.explanation: The signed correction identifies 12 as the updated figure.

questions.prompt: Two pages share the reference K4. One is dated May 3 and one May 8. Which detail distinguishes them?
questions.explanation: Both use K4, so the dates are the stated difference.

questions.prompt: Rule: confirmed facts carry a check mark. The file shows ✓ location, ? motive, ✓ time. Which fact remains uncertain?
questions.explanation: The question mark appears beside motive, while the other facts are checked.

stageGroups.title: Witness Words
stageGroups.encouragement: Words matter. Next, put every event in the only order the record allows.

questions.prompt: A witness says, ‘I heard the bell and then saw the door open.’ What happened first in that account?
questions.explanation: The word ‘then’ places the bell before the open door.

questions.prompt: Which statement reports an observation rather than a conclusion?
questions.explanation: A visible lamp state and time are observations; the other choices infer motives or judgment.

questions.prompt: A witness says, ‘Nora told me that Eli saw the package.’ Who is described as seeing it?
questions.explanation: The sentence attributes the sighting to Eli.

questions.prompt: Which question asks for a specific fact without suggesting the answer?
choices: What did you see after the lights changed?
The car was speeding, wasn't it?
You agree the bag was blue?
Why did the careless driver run?
questions.explanation: The open question requests an account without embedding a proposed answer.

questions.prompt: The exact quote is ‘about five minutes.’ Which summary preserves the uncertainty?
choices: The event lasted exactly five minutes
The event lasted more than ten minutes
The witness estimated roughly five minutes
questions.explanation: ‘About’ signals an estimate rather than an exact duration.

questions.prompt: One account says ‘before lunch’; another says ‘at 12:20.’ What is the clearest next step?
choices: Clarify the timing rather than assume they match
questions.explanation: The relationship between the two descriptions needs clarification before comparison.

questions.prompt: A witness corrects ‘Gate 6’ to ‘Gate 9.’ What should the accurate note show?
choices: The correction from Gate 6 to Gate 9
questions.explanation: Recording the correction preserves both accuracy and the change.

stageGroups.title: Timeline Test
stageGroups.encouragement: Chronology secured. Now test whether each conclusion is actually supported by its reasons.

questions.prompt: A meeting starts at 13:40 and lasts 35 minutes. When does it end?
questions.explanation: Adding 35 minutes to 13:40 gives 14:15.

questions.prompt: The call came 8 minutes before the 16:30 entry. When was the call?
questions.explanation: Eight minutes before 16:30 is 16:22.

questions.prompt: Sequence: document printed, envelope sealed, courier arrived, receipt signed. What happened immediately before the courier arrived?
questions.explanation: The sealed envelope directly precedes the courier in the given sequence.

questions.prompt: Event B occurred after A but before C. Which order must be correct?
questions.explanation: The two constraints place B between A and C.

questions.prompt: A camera log is 4 minutes fast. It shows 11:26. What is the corrected time?
questions.explanation: A clock four minutes fast displays four minutes later than the corrected time.

questions.prompt: The interview ended at 10:50 after lasting 25 minutes. When did it begin?
questions.explanation: Subtracting 25 minutes from 10:50 gives 10:25.

questions.prompt: A note was made after the call but before the email. Which item sits in the middle?
questions.explanation: The stated order is call, note, email.

stageGroups.title: Argument Anatomy
stageGroups.encouragement: Reasoning tested. The exhibits now start changing by a single decisive detail.

questions.prompt: Argument: All blue cards are valid. This card is blue. Therefore it is valid. What role does ‘This card is blue’ play?
questions.explanation: It supplies a fact used to reach the conclusion that the card is valid.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion follows? Every sealed box has a label. Box R is sealed.
questions.explanation: The general rule applies directly to sealed Box R.

questions.prompt: Claim: ‘The plan failed because it was Tuesday.’ What is missing?
choices: A reason connecting Tuesday to the failure
questions.explanation: The claim states a cause without explaining why that day would produce the failure.

questions.prompt: Which response addresses the argument rather than the speaker?
choices: The second premise is not supported by the file
questions.explanation: It evaluates the stated reasoning instead of attacking the person.

questions.prompt: Premise: If the alarm sounds, the light flashes. The light did not flash. What follows under the rule?
questions.explanation: Under the stated conditional rule, a sounding alarm would require a flashing light.

questions.prompt: Two explanations fit the facts. What is the strongest next move?
choices: Identify what additional fact would distinguish them
questions.explanation: A discriminating fact can test which explanation better fits the record.

questions.prompt: A conclusion repeats its premise in different words. What is the main weakness?
questions.explanation: Restating a claim does not provide a separate reason to accept it.

stageGroups.title: Exhibit Control
stageGroups.encouragement: Details under control. Next, ask questions that reveal information instead of planting it.

questions.prompt: Exhibit A: K7 · 08:40 · EAST. Exhibit B: K7 · 08:40 · WEST. Which field changes?
questions.explanation: The reference and time match; only EAST changes to WEST.

questions.prompt: A receipt shows 3 items at 12 units each. What total quantity is recorded?
questions.explanation: Three groups of 12 equal 36.

questions.prompt: Document 1 lists Ada, Bo, Chen. Document 2 lists Ada, Chen. Which name is absent from Document 2?
questions.explanation: Bo appears only in the first list.

questions.prompt: Map key: solid line = open route; dotted line = closed route. Route P is dotted. What does the key show?
questions.explanation: The map key explicitly assigns closed status to a dotted line.

questions.prompt: A photo label reads ‘Room 4, 18:05.’ The index reads ‘Room 4, 18:50.’ What needs checking?
questions.explanation: The room matches, while 18:05 and 18:50 conflict.

questions.prompt: Version 2 adds one sentence and removes none. It now has 9 sentences. How many did Version 1 have?
questions.explanation: If one sentence was added to reach nine, the earlier version had eight.

questions.prompt: Rule: use the latest verified version. V3 is verified at 15:00; V4 is unverified at 15:10. Which should be used now?
questions.explanation: V3 is the latest version that meets the stated verification rule.

stageGroups.title: Cross-Examination
stageGroups.encouragement: Questions sharpened. The next cases test fairness, honesty, and the limits of your role.

questions.prompt: Which question is clearest?
choices: Where were you standing when the bell rang?
Why was it all so strange?
questions.explanation: It asks for one specific fact tied to a defined moment.

questions.prompt: A reply does not answer the question. What is the most useful follow-up?
choices: Ask three new questions at once
Restate the question briefly and precisely
questions.explanation: A concise restatement gives the speaker a clear opportunity to answer the point.

questions.prompt: Which question contains two issues and should be split?
choices: When did you arrive and who was with you?
questions.explanation: It asks about both timing and company, which can be answered more clearly separately.

questions.prompt: A witness uses the word ‘nearby.’ What follow-up improves precision?
choices: About how far away were you?
questions.explanation: The question asks for a usable estimate without supplying one.

questions.prompt: Which approach best tests an apparent inconsistency?
choices: Accuse the witness of lying immediately
Put the two statements side by side and ask for clarification
questions.explanation: Direct comparison invites an explanation while keeping the discrepancy clear.

questions.prompt: The answer is ‘I don't remember.’ What should a fair questioner avoid?
choices: Pretending the witness gave a definite answer
Checking whether a record could help
questions.explanation: A lack of memory should not be rewritten as certainty.

questions.prompt: Which closing question checks completeness without suggesting new facts?
choices: You have now told us everything, correct?
The missing detail is the blue bag, isn't it?
Is there anything important about that moment that I have not asked?
You agree my summary must be right?
questions.explanation: It allows relevant omitted information without embedding a proposed answer.

stageGroups.title: Ethics & Scope
stageGroups.encouragement: Judgment intact. Now apply a fictional courtroom rulebook exactly as written.

questions.prompt: You discover a factual error in your own summary. What is the strongest response?
choices: Hide it because it is inconvenient
Correct it transparently and alert the appropriate people
questions.explanation: Transparent correction protects the accuracy and integrity of the record.

questions.prompt: A friend asks for confidential case details. What is the appropriate default?
choices: Do not share the private information
questions.explanation: A personal relationship does not remove the duty to protect private information.

questions.prompt: A task falls outside your competence. What should you do?
choices: Recognize the limit and seek suitable support
Pretend the issue does not exist
Delegate it to an unqualified friend
questions.explanation: Knowing when to seek support is part of responsible professional judgment.

questions.prompt: You notice a personal connection that could affect your independence. What is the best first step?
choices: Disclose it through the proper process
questions.explanation: Early disclosure allows the situation to be assessed openly and appropriately.

questions.prompt: Someone pressures you to state a fact more strongly than the evidence allows. What should guide you?
choices: Accuracy about what the evidence does and does not show
questions.explanation: Professional advocacy does not justify overstating the available support.

questions.prompt: A colleague respectfully identifies a missing source. What is the constructive response?
choices: Check the source and update the work if needed
questions.explanation: Checking a material concern strengthens accuracy and teamwork.

questions.prompt: A client asks for a guaranteed outcome. What is the honest response?
choices: Explain that an outcome cannot be guaranteed
questions.explanation: Uncertain outcomes should not be presented as guaranteed facts.

stageGroups.title: Objection Logic
stageGroups.encouragement: Rules applied. The hearing now speeds up and every priority competes for attention.

questions.prompt: Fictional rule: questions may address one event only. ‘When did you arrive and why did you leave?’ breaks which rule?
questions.explanation: The question joins arrival and departure despite the one-event rule.

questions.prompt: Rule: a claim is admissible only if tagged VERIFIED. Item M is tagged DRAFT. What is its status under the rule?
choices: Admissible because it has a tag
questions.explanation: The stated rule requires the specific VERIFIED tag, which Item M lacks.

questions.prompt: Rule: after a RED card, the next speaker must pause. A RED card appears. What must happen next?
questions.explanation: The consequence follows directly from the fictional RED-card rule.

questions.prompt: Rule A: direct observations use Box 1. Rule B: reported statements use Box 2. ‘I saw the door close’ belongs where?
questions.explanation: The sentence describes what the speaker personally saw.

questions.prompt: Rule: only the chair may extend time. A witness asks for five more minutes. Who can approve it?
questions.explanation: The fictional rule assigns that decision solely to the chair.

questions.prompt: Rule: an objection must name the broken rule. Which response complies?
choices: Objection: the question combines two events
questions.explanation: It identifies the specific one-event rule said to be broken.

questions.prompt: Rule: GREEN means continue; AMBER means clarify; RED means stop. The signal is AMBER. What should happen?
questions.explanation: AMBER is explicitly defined as a request for clarification.

stageGroups.title: Under Pressure
stageGroups.encouragement: Pressure handled. One final hearing combines evidence, timing, logic, and judgment.

questions.prompt: Thirty seconds remain and a quoted number conflicts with the exhibit. What should happen first?
choices: Check the number against the exhibit
questions.explanation: A material conflict should be checked before the number is relied upon.

questions.prompt: Two tasks arrive: correct a name that identifies the wrong person, or adjust a heading font. Which comes first?
questions.explanation: An error that points to the wrong person has greater immediate importance than formatting.

questions.prompt: An interruption makes you lose your place in a summary. What is the safest recovery?
choices: Return to the last confirmed point and restate the structure
questions.explanation: Returning to a known point prevents a hidden gap in the summary.

questions.prompt: A new verified fact undermines your preferred argument. What is the strongest response?
choices: Call the fact irrelevant without checking
Update the argument to account for it
questions.explanation: Sound reasoning must respond to material verified information, even when inconvenient.

questions.prompt: A note is urgent but its source label is missing. What balances speed and reliability?
choices: Confirm the source before relying on the note
questions.explanation: Urgency does not replace the need to establish where material information came from.

questions.prompt: Three points must be presented: strongest fact, supporting timeline, minor formatting issue. What order is clearest?
questions.explanation: The order leads with the central fact, then its support, and leaves the minor issue last.

questions.prompt: A speaker becomes faster and less clear. What is the best adjustment?
choices: Slow down, state one point, and signpost the next
questions.explanation: A controlled pace and visible structure improve clarity under pressure.

stageGroups.title: The Final Hearing
stageGroups.encouragement: Final hearing complete. Your advocate profile is ready for the reveal.

questions.prompt: Final file: the verified log says Gate C; an older draft says Gate A. Rule: use the latest verified source. Which gate should the summary use?
questions.explanation: The rule favors the verified log, which identifies Gate C.

questions.prompt: A witness estimates ‘ten to fifteen minutes.’ Which final submission is accurate?
choices: The witness said exactly ten minutes
The witness gave a range of ten to fifteen minutes
The witness said more than fifteen minutes
questions.explanation: The range should be preserved rather than converted into false precision.

questions.prompt: The timeline is call 14:05, arrival 14:18, note 14:22. How long passed from call to arrival?
questions.explanation: From 14:05 to 14:18 is thirteen minutes.

questions.prompt: Argument: every marked page was reviewed; Page 7 is marked. What follows?
questions.explanation: The stated general rule applies to marked Page 7.

questions.prompt: A private detail is irrelevant to the issue. What is the strongest professional choice?
choices: Leave it out and protect confidentiality
questions.explanation: Irrelevant private information should not be exposed for effect.

questions.prompt: One exhibit conflicts with your summary by a single digit. What should you do before presenting?
choices: Resolve the digit and correct the summary
questions.explanation: The conflict should be resolved so the presentation accurately reflects the exhibit.

questions.prompt: The facts are checked, the argument is structured, and one uncertainty remains clearly labeled. What is the best final move?
choices: Present the supported case and state the remaining uncertainty honestly
questions.explanation: Strong advocacy can be clear and persuasive without disguising the limits of the evidence.
